
To help make science more engaging and accessible, I led a live physics demonstration at St. Xavier's College, Kathmandu as part of SXPC Nepal on February 2, 2024. The event featured interactive stalls where students could observe and participate in experiments that illustrate core physics concepts in an intuitive, hands-on way.

One of the crowd favorites was the Chladni plate demonstration, where sound-driven vibrations produced intricate sand patterns on a metal plate — a beautiful visualization of mode shapes and resonance. We also presented demonstrations related to solid-state physics, discussing crystal structures and electrical conduction in materials, and showcased experiments in mechanics, optics, and electromagnetism to translate textbook theory into memorable experiences.

<div align="center"><img src="/blog_images/chladniplate.jpg" width="500" height="500"></div>
<div align="center"><img src="/blog_images/chladniplate2.jpg" width="500" height="500"></div>


The exhibition area included educational posters, diagrams of classic experiments, and stations where students could try simple measurements and observations themselves. Engagement was high: many students stopped to ask questions, interact with the setups, and try experiments firsthand.

Our primary goal was to spark curiosity and show that physics is not only theoretical but also deeply connected to everyday phenomena. By turning abstract concepts into interactive demonstrations, we aimed to make learning more intuitive and inspire students to explore science further.
